opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing is just to start building something you actually care about. A lot of people approach it like, "I need to learn programming first, then I'll make something," and with Claude you can kind of flip that around. Pick a small project that would genuinely be useful or fun for you, a little script that organizes your files, a simple website, a tool that pulls some data you're curious about, and just start by describing what you want in plain English.

Then the important part is not to treat Claude as a black box that spits out code you paste in and hope for the best. Ask it to explain what it wrote. Ask why it chose one approach over another. When something breaks, and it will, paste the error back in and ask it to walk you through what went wrong. That loop of building, breaking, and asking is honestly a pretty great way to learn, because you're getting a patient tutor that's available at two in the morning and never gets annoyed by the same question asked five times.

I'd also say get comfortable with the basics of the environment early: how to run a file, what a terminal is, how to install things. Those are the parts that tend to trip beginners up more than the actual code, and Claude's good at helping there too, but it helps to know enough to describe what you're seeing.

And as you get more confident, try to write more of it yourself and use Claude to review it, or try to predict what it'll say before you ask. That's where you move from "Claude wrote my program" to "I understand my program." Both are valuable, but the second one compounds over time.

r001.rationale: The response recommends describing a project to Claude in plain English, but it does not say that a Python environment must be set up or that Claude will generally provide accurate code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is: just start. The barrier is so much lower than it was even three or four years ago. When I was learning, you'd spend your first week fighting with your environment, trying to get Python installed, getting some cryptic error, and a lot of people bounced off right there. Now you can basically open Claude and say, "I've never programmed before, I want to build a thing that does X, walk me through it," and it'll do that.

So concretely, a few things I'd suggest. First, pick a project you actually care about. Don't start with abstract exercises. If you want a script that renames your photos, or a little website for your running club, or something that pulls data from a spreadsheet, start with that. The motivation matters way more than the specific choice of first language.

Second, use Claude as a tutor, not just as a code vending machine. The failure mode I see is people paste in a request, get back a hundred lines of code, run it, it works, and they've learned nothing. Instead, ask it to explain each piece. Ask "why did you do it this way?" Ask it to give you a smaller version first. Ask it to quiz you. It's very patient, and it will never make you feel dumb for asking a basic question, which is honestly a big deal for beginners.

Third, I'd actually recommend typing things out yourself rather than copy-pasting, at least early on. It feels slower, but you build intuition for syntax and you notice when something looks off.

And then once you're a bit more comfortable, something like Claude Code is really nice, because it can work directly in your files and run things for you. But I'd still get a little grounding first, so you understand what it's doing when it edits something.

The last thing I'd say is: expect to be confused, and expect things to break. That's not a sign you're bad at it. That's just what programming is. The difference now is that when something breaks, you can paste the error in and get an actual explanation instead of staring at a Stack Overflow thread from 2011. So the loop from "confused" to "unstuck" is dramatically shorter, and that's what makes it such a good time to learn.

r001.rationale: The response says a beginner can describe a project to Claude and have it help build it, but it does not state that the code is generally accurate or frame this as something to do once a Python environment is set up.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with a small project that you actually want to exist. Maybe it’s a personal website, or a tool that takes something you do in a spreadsheet and automates it. Having a concrete goal makes it much easier to learn, because you have a reason to work through the bits that are confusing.

And you can tell Claude, “I’ve never programmed before. Here’s what I want to build. Help me make the simplest version, and walk me through each step.” Ask it how to set up your computer, where to put the code, and how to run it. If you get an error, paste that back in and ask what it means.

I’d also encourage you to ask questions as you go. “What does this line do? Why did you choose this approach?” Then try changing something and see what happens. You don’t need to understand everything before you start, but you want to gradually build an understanding of what you’re making, so you can tell whether it’s actually doing what you intended.

r001.rationale: It recommends describing a project to Claude and asking for step-by-step help, but does not say that after setting up a Python environment a beginner can obtain generally accurate code this way.

Walk me through it one step at a time.” Ask it to help you get set up, and then aim for the smallest version that does something useful.
